title: Dear Sir or Hey Dude?
intro: Formal, neutral, informal — the register of a single phrase can make or break an email before anyone reads past the greeting.

A2.right: informal greeting — fine for friends, family and most colleagues
A2.why: “Hi” is the everyday friendly greeting; safe almost anywhere except very formal letters.

A2.right: formal greeting — you know the person's name
A2.why: Use “Dear” + title + surname when you know who will read it.

A2.right: informal closing — you expect to meet in person
A2.why: “See” tells the reader you plan to meet face to face.

A2.right: neutral-formal closing — safe for almost any work email
A2.why: If in doubt at work, “Best regards” never offends anyone.

A2.right: very informal greeting — close friends only, never a boss
A2.why: “Hey” is very relaxed; to your boss it can sound rude.
One word with an exclamation mark: friendly and casual.
The full form, with “very much”, sounds careful and professional.

A2.right: informal closing — wishing the person well
A2.why: A warm goodbye: you hope the person stays well.

A2.right: formal greeting — you don't know the person's name
A2.why: No name? Use “Dear Sir or Madam”, never “Dear Señor”.
A short, polite way to say you took a while to answer.

A2.right: very informal closing — family and partners only
A2.why: “Love” is for people you love; never use it with a client.

A2.left: Could you send me the prices, please?
A2.right: neutral — a polite request in a short email
A2.why: “Could you … please?” is polite but simple: perfect for a shop or hotel.

B1.left: I hope this email finds you well.
B1.right: formal opening line — wishing the reader well
B1.why: A classic polite first line in professional emails.
A chatty question you'd ask a friend, not a bank.

B1.right: formal sign-off — you began with the person's name (Dear Ms Ruiz)
B1.why: Memory hook: Sincerely goes with a known name (S and S).

B1.right: formal sign-off — you began with Dear Sir or Madam
B1.why: No name at the start? Finish with “faithfully”.

B1.right: informal goodbye — you'll talk again soon
B1.why: Relaxed spoken English; fine with friends, odd in a formal email.

B1.left: I look forward to hearing from you.
B1.right: formal — the last line, politely asking for a reply
B1.why: The standard formal way to say “please write back”.

B1.right: informal — casually starting your main point
B1.why: “Just” makes it light and friendly, with no formal build-up.
Office English for “here's the file”; not “I attach you”.

B1.left: Thanks for getting back to me.
B1.right: neutral — thanking someone for their reply
B1.why: “Get back to someone” means reply; a friendly, neutral opener.

B1.right: neutral — politely interrupting someone with a request
B1.why: You apologise for taking their time before you ask.

B1.right: informal — asking a friend to write to you
B1.why: “A line” is a short message; casual and warm.

B1.left: I am sorry to inform you that...
B1.why: “Inform” sounds official, so the bad news arrives politely.

B2.left: I am writing to enquire about...
B2.right: formal first line — explaining you want information
B2.why: “Enquire” is the formal British verb for “ask about”.

B2.right: informal — warning the reader the message is short
B2.why: Casual signal that you won't take much of their time.

B2.left: I would be grateful if you could...
B2.right: formal — politely asking someone to do something for you
B2.why: Much softer than “Send me…”: the conditional makes it polite.
Friendly way to say “it's not a problem”.

B2.left: Please do not hesitate to contact me.
B2.why: Formal email code for “just ask me”.

B2.left: Let me know if that works for you.
B2.right: neutral — checking a plan or time suits the reader
B2.why: Polite but relaxed: you leave the final word to them.

B2.right: informal-neutral — a casual closing common in British emails
B2.why: Very British: means “thanks, bye” between people who know each other.

B2.right: formal — hoping what you sent meets their needs
B2.why: A formal, slightly stiff way to close after giving information.

B2.left: Apologies for the delay in replying.
B2.right: formal — saying sorry for a slow answer
B2.why: The noun “apologies” sounds more formal than “sorry”.
Friendly exaggeration; lovely with friends, too much for a client.

B2.left: I am afraid I will be unable to attend.
B2.right: formal — politely saying you can't come
B2.why: “I'm afraid” softens bad news; “unable to attend” is formal for “can't come”.

B2.left: Following up on my previous email,
B2.right: neutral — gently reminding someone who hasn't replied
B2.why: A polite nudge: no blame, just a reminder.

C1.left: I am writing on behalf of...
C1.right: formal — introducing yourself as a representative
C1.why: “On behalf of” = speaking for a person or group, like “en nombre de”.

C1.right: formal — linking back to a talk or phone call you had
C1.why: Formal way to continue something you discussed out loud.

C1.left: Should you require any further information,
I would like to draw your attention to...
C1.why: You “draw attention” to something you want them to notice.

C1.right: very formal — a slightly stiff way to inform someone
C1.why: Common in official notices; many people find it rather cold.

C1.right: informal — casual way to invite someone to reach out
C1.why: No actual shouting: it just means “tell me”.

C1.left: With reference to your email of...
C1.right: formal — naming the date of their earlier email
C1.why: Usually followed by a date: “of 3 March”.

C1.left: I trust you are keeping well.
C1.why: Elegant British opening; “trust” here means “hope and believe”.

C1.left: Pending your approval, we will proceed.
C1.right: formal — saying you'll act once they agree
C1.why: “Pending” = until it arrives; nothing happens without their yes.

C1.left: Bear with me on this one.
C1.right: informal — asking for patience while you sort something out
C1.why: “Bear with me” = be patient with me; not the animal!

C1.left: I regret to inform you that...
C1.right: formal — opening a piece of bad news
C1.why: The most formal way to deliver bad news: rejections, cancellations.

C1.left: Happy to jump on a call.
C1.right: neutral, modern — offering a quick phone or video chat
C1.why: Modern office English: “jump on a call” = have a quick call.
